newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Investigators dig up Brcko mass grave in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Investigators dig up Brcko mass grave in Bosnia.

text.p: Experts are exhuming a suspected mass grave linked to the alleged 1992 massacre of Moslems and Croats at a Serb prison camp in the north Bosnian town of Brcko, the U.N. war crimes tribunal said on Tuesday.

A team of 25 forensic specialists began the dig in Bosnia's post-war Serb republic under the protection of the NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR), said the tribunal, which is based in The Hague.

The excavation relates to a 1995 indictment in which U.N. prosecutors say that hundreds of Moslem and Croat men were systematically killed at the Serb-run Luka camp in Brcko at the outset of Bosnia's 1992-95 war.
Suspected camp commander Goran Jelisic was charged with genocide and another Serb, Ranko Cesic, with crimes against humanity. Both remain at large.
Jelisic stands accused of 16 murders, allegedly committed during a genocidal campaign of "ethnic cleansing", or mass expulsion and murder, in the area.

"He introduced himself as the 'Serb Adolf', said that he had come to Brcko to kill Moslems and often informed the Moslem detainees and others of the number of Moslems he had killed," the indictment issued against him said.
Cesic, accused of 13 murders, is also alleged to have held a position of authority at the Luka camp.
The opening of the grave is meant to help corroborate evidence in the charges against the two men.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia said Brcko was the sixth mass grave site in the region to be exhumed by ICTY forensic specialists.
Last year the tribunal opened graves containing the victims of an alleged Serb massacre in the Bosnian Moslem enclave of Srebrenica in July 1995.

It also excavated a grave near the Croatian town of Vukovar containing victims of a massacre of Croat hospital patients after the Serbian-led Yugoslav federal army took the town in Croatia's 1991 independence war.

"The majority of the 650 victims recovered (from graves exhumed to date) died from multiple gunshot wounds. Some were found with their hands bound and a number had been blindfolded prior to execution," it said.
The tribunal said it needed $2.2 million to carry out its exhumations programme for this year.
About half of this amount has already been raised through contributions from Austria, Canada, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland and the United States.
Created by the U.N. Security Council in May 1993, the tribunal has so far publicly indicted 78 suspects -- 57 Serbs, 18 Croats and three Moslems.
Two of these have been convicted and sentenced and a further eight are in the tribunal's custody. Two died before they could stand trial and the remaining 66, most of them Serbs, are still at large.
The tribunal has no police force of its own and relies on the former Yugoslav republics, other states or international troops in Bosnia to make arrests.
The two most prominent suspects on the tribunal's wanted list are former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and the former Bosnian Serb military commander, General Ratko Mladic.
Both men have been charged with the genocide of Bosnian Moslems and both remain at large.
